children: HP Inc. won't issue fiscal-year guidance just yet, citing an industry-wide slump in personal computer unit volumes that it expects to persist through 2027.

The company said in a securities filing Monday that it remains in its "planning period" and consequently isn't issuing guidance for the next fiscal year. That on its own is unsurprising: The phrasing mirrors language from last month's earnings call, when Chief Financial Officer Karen Parkhill said it was too early to provide an outlook.

The impetus appears to be falling PC unit volumes. While HP noted Monday that it remains "premature" to detail its upcoming fiscal year outlook, it projects industry-wide volumes will decline by a mid-single-digit percentage in calendar year 2027 compared to 2026.
Shares fell 3.9% to $33.05 on Monday and were the worst performers in the S&P 500. The benchmark index was up 0.9%.
U.S.- listed shares of Lenovo Group, which designs and manufactures personal computers, fell 5.3%.

The confluence of a memory-chip shortage and soaring costs has forced HP and its peers to sell fewer devices at higher prices. Sales of personal computers and laptops, which account for roughly 70% of the company's overall revenue, have come under increasing pressure.

On the latest earnings call, management noted that rising input costs were exerting near-term pressure on operating margins, particularly within HP's Personal Systems business. Although overall revenue rose, personal systems unit sales fell 16% for the period, led by a 19% drop in consumer units. That marks a sharp deceleration from the second quarter, when sales declined by 7% and 8%, respectively.

Interim CEO Bruce Dale Broussard told analysts the company continues to "effectively execute" its mitigation plan. "We remain confident in our memory and storage supply availability for this fiscal year, and our focus on our needs into next year and beyond," he said.
HP is slated to update investors on its cost-mitigation efforts in its fiscal fourth-quarter report.
